parties:
Professor Golam Azam   ----- Petitioner.
Vs.
Government of Bangladesh and others  ----- Respondents.
full_judgment:
2. It is stated in the petition that the petitioner, Prof. Golam Azam, is a Bangladeshi citizen by birth having been born at Dhaka on the 22nd November, 1922; that his father late Moulana Ghulam Kabir was born in village Birgram, Police Station Nabinagar, District Comilla now Brahmanbaria and from generations they are permanent residents in the terriories now comprised in Bangladesh; that the petitioner passed the Intermediate Examination from the Islamia Intermediate Government College, Dhaka and then obtained his Graduation and his Masters Degree in Political Science from the University of Dhaka; that the petitioner was General Secretary of the Student's Union of the then Fazlul Huq Muslim Hall and he was also General Secretary of the Dhaka University Students Union wherein he played a very vital role in the Bengali Language Movement and as the General Secretary of the Dhaka University Students Union; the petitioner read a memorandum before the then Prime Minister of Pakistan on the 27th of November, 1948 at the Gymnasium ground of the Dhaka University urging him to make Bengali as one of the State Languages, as one of the main demands; that the petitioner was a professor of Political Science for five years in the Carmichael College, Rangpur; that he fought for restoration of democracy during the Ayub regime and was General Secretary of the Eastern Wing of the Pakistan Democratic Movement (PDM); that because of his active role in various democratic movements the petitioner was arrested once in 1955, then in 1964 but he was released by the order of the Dhaka High Court on Habeas Corpus petition; that the petitioner dedicated his life for the establishment of Islamic Social Justice in all spheres of the society and he became the Ameer (President) of the Jamaat-e-Islami of the then East Pakistan in 1969; that in the General Election of 1970 Jamaat-e-Islami took part in the election and obtained the second highest votes, next to the Awami League in the then East Pakistan; that from the election of 1970 political rivalry and enmity developed between the Jamaat-e-Islami and the Awami League and the petitioner being the head of the Jamaat-e-Islami became the target of the Awami League, which later on, formed the first Government in the independent Bangladesh; that in spite of political differences with Awami League the petitioner advocated for transfer of power to the Awami League as it obtained the highest number of seats in the then National Assembly; that during the liberation struggle the petitioner was actively engaged in helping people and saving them from the military atrocities of Yahya regime, but even then the Awami League considered the petitioner their arch enemy; that the petitioner was a resident of Bangladesh on the 25th of March, 1971 and he continued to be so resident and on the 22nd of November, 1971 he went to Lahore for attending his party's central working committee meeting and on the 3rd of December, 1971 the petitioner was returning to Dhaka by plane but the plane could not land at Dhaka Airport because of the war and as such the plane at first landed at Colombo and as there was bombing at that time at Karachi Airport the plane went to Jeddah where the petitioner remained a few days wherefrom he was sent back to Karachi along with the other passengers; that the petitioner had to remain in Pakistan against his will for some months as the then Government of Pakistan did not allow any Bangladeshi citizen to leave Pakistan, that the petitioner tried to go to London in the month of March, 1972 for making contact with his family but failed to obtain any travel document in Pakistan and thereafter arranged a Pakistani passport to go to Hajj in the month of December, 1972; that the petitioner during the Hajj met friends & acquaintances from Bangladesh who went for Hajj who informed him about a political mis-propaganda against the petitioner in Bangladesh; that thereafter the petitioner went to London in the first week of April, 1973 where he came to learn from a news item published in the Bangladesh Observer to the effect that he along with 38 others were declared by a notification dated 18.4.73 of the Department of Home Affairs of Bangladesh to be disqualified to become citizen of Bangladesh. 

 3. It is also stated in the petition that the petitioner found it impossible to return to Bangladesh and he stayed in England against his will but 1ie never went to Pakistan nor he obtained nationality or citizenship of any other country; that after the publication of the impugned notification dated 18.4.73 the petitioner continued to reside in England since the first week of April, 1973; that in the meantime in 1975 there was a change of Government and the political situation in Bangladesh; and the new Government of Bangladesh by a notification dated 17.1.76 (Annexure-C) invited applications from those persons whose citizenship was cancelled by the previous Government for restoration of their citizenship and accordingly the petitioner sent an application on 20.5.76 to the Secretary, Ministry of Home Affairs, Bangladesh praying for restoration of his citizenship but having received no reply the petitioner sent another application on 12.1.77 to the Chief Martial Law Administrator renewing his prayer for restoration of citizenship but the petitioner received a reply from the Ministry of Home Affairs dated 23.4.77 (Annexure-E) to the following effect: 

 "With reference to your application dated 12.1.77 addressed to the Chief Martial Law Administrator, Government of Bangladesh, I am directed to inform you that the Government of the People's Republic of Bangladesh regret their inability to accede to your request to restore Bangladesh Citizenship". 

 4. The petitioner also received a letter dated 29.9.77 from the office of the High Commissioner for Bangladesh in England (Annexure-E 1) to the same effect; that in the meantime the petitioner lost his father in 1973 and his old mother applied on 14.11.77 to the Government of Bangladesh praying for restoration of the citizenship to the petitioner which was refused but the Ministry of Home Affairs, Government of Bangladesh by their letter dated 11.3.78 expressed their no objection for granting visa to the petitioner to see his ailing mother and accordingly the petitioner obtained visa from London and entered Bangladesh on 11.7.78 with a visa for three months; that after his arrival in Bangladesh on 11.7.78 the petitioner was registered by the concerned authority as a Foreigner; that the petitioner obtained extension of his visa twice and then in order to avoid possible ouster from the court he filed an application for registration as a citizen of Bangladesh to the Ministry of Home Affairs on 8.11.78 surrendering his Pakistani passport to the authority concerned, that thereafter the petitioner has been permanently residing in Bangladesh considering himself a citizen of Bangladesh by birth; that on 27.5.80 some members of the Parliament inquired from the Government about the stay of the petitioner in Bangladesh on which the then Minister for Home Affairs, Government of Bangladesh made a statement in the Parliament to the effect that the petitioner had filed an application praying for registration as a citizen of Bangladesh by surrendering his Pakistani passport and that the matter is pending decision of the Government; that thereafter the Ministry of Home Affairs, Immigration Section vide letter dated 28.4.81 asked the petitioner to submit an affidavit with oath of allegiance to Bangladesh and the petitioner submitted the required affidavit on 30.4.81; that after a long silence the petitioner received a letter dated 3.12.86 from the Ministry of Home Affairs (Annexure H-1) requesting him to let the Ministry to know as to why he was staying in Bangladesh without visa since he had not approached the authority for extension of visa after he had registered his name with the Foreigners Registration Office on 12.7.78 to which the petitioner sent a reply on 22.12.86 (Annexure H-2) asserting himself as a citizen of Bangladesh by birth and informing that on 8.11.78 he made an application for restoration of his citizenship by surrendering his passport and that his application was under the active consideration of the authorities; that the petitioner also asserted himself as a citizen of Bangladesh in a Press Conference held on 30.5.88; that the name of the petitioner was also published in the voter list published on 5.8.83 (Annexure-M) as well as in the voter list published on 15.2.90 (Annexure-I); that the petitioner thought that the clouds about his citizenship was over and he was a citizen of Bangladesh; that the petitioner was elected as the Chief of his party, Jamaat-e-Islami of Bangladesh, and after the general election held in 1991 the Prime Minister personally met the petitioner for the support of his party before formation of the Government and during the election of the President both the candidates for the office of President of the country also requested him for the support of his party; that all an a sudden the petitioner received a notice dated 23.3.92 (Annexure-K) from the Ministry of Home Affairs, Immigration Branch to show cause by 10 AM of 24th of March, 1992 why the petitioner should not be deported from Bangladesh and why other legal actions should not be taken against him as he had been disqualified to be the citizen of Bangladesh by a Notification dated 18.4.73 and he is a registered Foreigner and as he became the Ameer of Jamaat-e-Islami, Bangladesh in contravention of Article 38 of the Constitution of the People's Republic of Bangladesh, to which the petitioner gave a reply on 24.3.92 (Annexure K-1) asserting his right as a citizen of Bangladesh and denying the allegations made in the show cause notice and also soliciting for personal hearing in the matter; but the respondent No. 1 illegally arrested the petitioner and detained him at the Dhaka Central Jail by issuing an order of detention dated 24.3.92 under section 3 of the Foreigners Act, 1946; that the petitioner sent a demand for justice notice to the respondent No.1 (Annexure-L) and thereafter challenged the order of detention by filing Writ Petition No. 1148 of 1992 on which a Rule was issued on 30.3.92. 

 6. The respondent No. 1 controverted the statements of the petitioner made in the petition by filing an affidavit-in-opposition wherein it is stated that the petitioner and his fore-fathers were born in the territory now comprised in Bangladesh but he is "now" not a citizen of Bangladesh as he has been staying abroad since before the liberation of Bangladesh; that the petitioner had actively participated in the anti-Bangladeshi campaign both inside and outside the country during the war of liberation and he continued to be a citizen of Pakistan that Armed Cadre of Jamaat-e-Islami such as Rajaker, Al-Badr and Al-Shams were placed under the disposal of Pakistan Army in the then East Pakistan during the war of liberation; that as the petitioner had actively participated in the Anti-liberation Movement the Government of Bangladesh disqualified him from being a citizen of Bangladesh by the impugned Notification (Annexure-B); that the people of Bangladesh are well aware about the role of the petitioner during the war of liberation who actively collaborated with Pakistani Army in raising the Rajakers, Al-Badr and Al-Shams, that the conduct of the petitioner makes it clear that he placed the Jamaat-e-Islami at the disposal of Pakistan Army; that it was not true that the petitioner was staying in Pakistan against his will, that it was also not true that the petitioner went to Saudi Arabia in 1972 for the purpose of performing Hajj but his mission to Saudi Arabia was to orchestrate anti-Bangladesh sentiment and he lobbied actively to dissuade the Muslim countries from recognizing Bangladesh as an independent state; that in the year 1972 the petitioner had organized "East Pakistan Recovery Committee" in Lahore; that in the same year the petitioner attended the Islamic Youth Conference in Riadh wherein he appealed to all of them to join in liberation struggle for recapturing East Pakistan and he had also organized a committee for recapturing East Pakistan in London; that in 1973 the petitioner went to Bengali in Libya to attend the conference of the Foreign Ministers of the Islamic countries and there he made an appeal not to recognize Bangladesh as an independent State; that the petitioner met the Saudi Badsha for seven times from 1973 to 1976 for not giving recognition to Bangladesh; that the Government being satisfied about the conduct of the petitioner passed the impugned order (Annexure-B); that during his stay in the United Kingdom after the liberation of Bangladesh he did not endeavor to obtain citizenship of Bangladesh and for his conduct and continuous citizenship of Pakistan he was declared not to be citizen of Bangladesh by the impugned notification dated 18.4.73 which was published in the Bangladesh Gazette on 22.6.73; that the petitioner went abroad before the liberation of Bangladesh and he did not submit his oath of allegiance to Bangladesh as he continued to be the citizen of Pakistan; that immediately after the liberation of Bangladesh as many as 14187 persons living in the United Kingdom obtained Bangladeshi Passport by surrendering their Pakistani Passport but the petitioner did not make any attempt to obtain Bangladeshi Passport and he remained as a Pakistani citizen in London; that the impugned notification dated 18.4.73 disqualifying the petitioner and 38 persons from being citizen of Bangladesh was issued in accordance with the provision of Article 3 of PO 149 of 1972; that the petitioner was permitted to travel to Bangladesh as a foreign national to see his ailing mother after his prayer for citizenship of Bangladesh was turned down twice by the Government; that the entry of the petitioner in Bangladesh was admittedly as a Pakistani citizen and he continued to stay in Bangladesh as a registered foreign national; that the petitioner came to Bangladesh with Pakistani Passport which was issued by Pakistan Embassy in London on 11.1.77, that the petitioner applied to the Government of Pakistan for his Passport affirming that he was a Pakistani National and he obtained extension of his visa twice in Bangladesh as a Pakistani national and thereby admitted himself to be a Pakistani national even in the year 1978, that the petitioner applied to the Ministry of Home Affairs for Bangladeshi citizenship and his application for Citizenship of Bangladesh was not supported by oath of allegiance as required by law; that the petitioner cannot be considered as a Bangladeshi Citizen as he had been staying in Bangladesh after registering himself as a Foreign national on his arrival with a Pakistani Passport; that the petitioner did not submit oath of allegiance voluntarily when he applied for restoration of citizenship of Bangladesh but on the asking of the Government he submitted his oath of allegiance on 30.4.81, that the petitioner was staying in Bangladesh illegally without extending his visa for which he was asked to show cause in 1986 and that non-consideration of his application for citizenship for a long time would not entitle the petitioner to be a citizen of Bangladesh. 

 7. It is also stated in the affidavit-in- opposition that the petitioner knew very well that he was residing in Bangladesh as a foreign national by registering himself as a foreign national and he had only applied for his citizenship and as such his enrollment as a voter was a bonafide mistake due to concealment of facts about his foreign nationality; that the selection of the petitioner as Ameer of Jamaat-e-Islami of Bangladesh was illegal, he being a foreign national and he became the head of the political party to destabilise the sovereignty of Bangladesh; that the fact that the Presidential Candidate went to the petitioner for his support would not ipso facto entitle the petitioner to be a citizen of Bangladesh; that the petitioner by his conduct had renounced his citizenship of Bangladesh and thereby he is disqualified to be a citizen of Bangladesh; that the application challenging the impugned notification (Annexure-B) is not tenable in law, rather such a belated application is liable to be rejected; that the petitioner came to Bangladesh with Pakistani Passport and he was registered as a foreign national; that he was disqualified to be a citizen of Bangladesh due to anti-Bangladesh activities and unseeming conduct; that the petitioner's continued stay in Bangladesh as a foreign national without any visa was illegal and that is why he was asked by the Government to explain as to how he was staying in Bangladesh; and as the reasons shown in his reply were not tenable in law, the Government took action under the Foreigners Act 1946 and that the impugned notification Annexure-B was issued neither malafide nor with any political motive or for any collateral purpose. 

 8. In the affidavit-in-reply it is stated that on the 26th of March, 1971 the petitioner became a citizen of Bangladesh by operation of law and continued to be a citizen of Bangladesh; that he had genuine political difference with Awami League, the party which formed the Government in 1972 but he did not participate in the anti-Bangladeshi campaign inside or outside Bangladesh; that it was denied that the petitioner or the Jamaat-e-Islami had any organizational link with Razakar, AI-Shams or Al-Badr, that the domicile of origin of the petitioner being the territories comprised in Bangladesh his position as a citizen of Bangladesh is protected; that the petitioner's case falls in the same category as that of 38 other people who were also disqualified to be citizen of Bangladesh and anyone of them applied for citizenship was readily granted the same; that on the 30th of November, 1973 the then Awami League Government granted a clemency to the persons who were convicted or accused of offences under the Bangladesh Collaborators (Special Tribunal) Order 1972; that the petitioner reiterated the statements made in paragraph 2-12 of the petition and denied the allegation that he played any heinous role during the war of independence. It is also stated that the petitioner could not be held responsible for the alleged rape, arson, looting and genocide, committed by the Pakistan Army. He also denied that during the Hajj in 1972 the petitioner made any anti-Bangladeshi campaign to dissuade the Muslim countries from giving recognition to Bangladesh or that he organised "East Pakistan Recovery Committee" in Lahore in that year or went to Bengazi in Libya for making any appeal to the Foreign Ministers Conference of Islamic Countries not to recognise Bangladesh or the petitioner met the king of Saudi Arabia seven times as alleged. It is also stated therein that under compulsion the petitioner had to retain his Pakistani Passport as a travel document in a foreign country as England. It is also denied that the petitioner entered Bangladesh as a Pakistani citizen and he merely used Pakistani Passport as a travel document; on the other hand, at the earliest opportunity he surrendered his Pakistani Passport to the Bangladesh authority by making fresh application for citizenship; that the petitioner did not enclose his oath of allegiance with the application for citizenship because he was not asked to do so; that it was also denied that the petitioner could not reconcile with the existence of Bangladesh; that it was also denied that the petitioner is a foreign national or he concealed his status for which voter lists were prepared due to bonafide mistake; it is also stated therein that Article 3 of PO 149 of 1972 was ultra vires of the Constitution inasmuch it did not provide any guideline to the executive for the exercise of the power under that Article. 

 9. It is contended by Mr. AR Yusuf, the learned Advocate appearing on behalf of the petitioner, that the petitioner, his father and his grand-father having been born in the territories now comprised in Bangladesh, the petitioner is a citizen of Bangladesh by birth from the date of coming of Bangladesh into existence on 26.3.71 according to the provisions of the Bangladesh Laws Continuance and Enforcement Order 1971, Bangladesh (Adaptation of Existing Laws) Order 1972 (PO 48 of 1972), the Citizenship Act 1951 and the PO 149 of 1972 and as such the impugned Notification dated 18.4.73 was illegal, malafide and motivated by political enmity. The learned Advocate has also contended that the impugned notification under Article 3 of PO 149 of 1972 having been made without giving any opportunity to the petitioner to explain his position the same was bad in law being contrary to the principle of natural justice. The learned Advocate has further contended that Article 3 of PO 149 of 1972 having conferred uncontrolled and unfettered discretion amounting to discrimination the said Article is violative of Articles 27 and 31 of the Constitution of the People's Republic of Bangladesh inasmuch as it has not provided any principle or guideline for the exercise of the power given to the Government. 

 Provided that the Government may notify in the Official Gazette any person or categories of persons to whom this Article shall not apply- 

 (2) The Government may grant citizenship of Bangladesh to any person who is a citizen of any state of Europe or North America or of any other state which the Government may by notification in the Official Gazette specify in this behalf. 

 3. In case of doubt as to whether a person is qualified to be deemed to be a citizen of Bangladesh under Article 2 of this Order the question shall be decided by the Government which decision shall be final. 

 4. The Government may, upon an application made to it in this behalf in the manner prescribed, grant citizenship to any/person. 

 4A. The Government may upon an application, made to it in this behalf in the manner prescribed, grant right of permanent residence to any person on such conditions as may be prescribed. 

 5. The Government may make rules for carrying out the purpose of this Order." 

 Now, therefore, the Government declares under Article 3 of the Bangladesh Citizenship (Temporary Provisions) Order 1972 (PO 149 of 1972), that the persons specified below do not qualify themselves to be the citizens of Bangladesh:— 

 by Order of the Government 

 "The contention of the respondents that Mr. Hamidul Huq Chowdhury was a citizen of Pakistan is based upon firstly, that he was away from Bangladesh and then by a notification dated 18.4.73 the Government declared that Mr. Hamidul Huq Chowdhury did not qualify to be a citizen of Bangladesh. Mr. Hamidul Huq Chowdhury claimed that he never became a citizen of any other state and his citizenship by statutory provision continued to be Bangladeshi. It appears to us on a perusal of the notification dated 18.4.73 that prior to the said notification Mr. Hamidul Huq Chowdhury by statutory provisions was a citizen of Bangladesh. This notification, however, was subsequently declared void by another notification of the Government dated 19.7.1977. In this view we hold that Mr. Hamidul Huq Chowdhury continued to be a citizen of Bangladesh though he was away from the country." 

 24. The learned Advocate for the petitioner laid much stress on the observation made by their Lordships as quoted above as the late Mr. Hamidul Haq Chowdhury was also one of the 39 persons to whom the impugned notification dated 1.8.4.73 (Annexure-B) was issued. That case related to the taking over of the newspapers, the Bangladesh Observer, Purbadesh and the Weekly Chitrali as abandoned property. In that case one of the contentions of the Government was that Mr. and Mrs. Hamidul Huq Chowdhury were the share- holders of the majority shares of those concerns and since late Mr. Hamidul Huq Chowdhury was living in Pakistan those properties were declared to be abandoned and at the hearing of that case it was mentioned that by the impugned order dated 18.4.73 late Mr. Hamidul Huq Chowdhury was deemed to be not a citizen of Bangladesh and he was continuing as a citizen of Pakistan. Against that contention the subsequent notification dated 19.7.77 was produced to show that the notification dated 18.4.73. So far as it related to Mr. Hamidul Huq Chowdhury was corrected by the subsequent notification cancelling the previous one. There was no determination of citizenship nor any issue was there before their Lordships as to whether late Chowdhury acquired citizenship of Bangladesh. Hence I am of the view that the observations made by their Lordships in that case is of no help to the learned Advocate for the petitioner in support of his contention that the petitioner acquired citizenship of Bangladesh by the statutory provision of PO 149 of 1972 inasmuch as the notification dated 18.4.73 has not been cancelled or withdrawn by the Government so far as the petitioner is concerned nor the observations can be taken as an authority for the proposition that prior to the notification dated 18.4.73 the petitioner continued to be a citizen of Bangladesh. 

 25. The next case referred to by the learned Advocate for the petitioner is the case of Muktar Ahmed Vs. Government of Bangladesh and others reported in 34 DLR 29. In that case Muktar Ahmed had migrated from India to the then East Pakistan on 28.2.51 and got himself along with the members of his family domiciled in the then East Pakistan by obtaining domicile certificates on 25.9.52. During liberation war he remained in Bangladesh althrough and on 29.4.72 he swore an affidavit affirming his allegiance to Bangladesh; but due to the prevailing situations he filed an application to the National Committee of Red Cross for going to Pakistan but he did not pursue that application which was rejected later on. He applied for formal citizenship certificate on 17.3.75 which was refused by the Government and he filed a Writ Petition challenging the order of the Government refusing to grant him citizenship certificate. In view of provision of Article 2 of PO 149 of 1972 and in view of the admitted fact of that case their Lordships held that he became a citizen of Bangladesh by operation of law. Their Lordships further held that the mere fact that he filed an application for going over to Pakistan cannot take away his citizenship. Thus the question before their Lordships was whether Muktar Ahmed lost his citizenship of Bangladesh by merely filing an application for going" over to Pakistan and their Lordships answered the question in the negative because Muktar Ahmed has all the three qualifications to be deemed to be a citizen of Bangladesh inasmuch as he was a permanent resident of Bangladesh on the 25th day of March, 1971, he continued to be so resident in Bangladesh and he was not otherwise declared to be disqualified for being a citizen of Bangladesh under any law. As such it has been held that his citizenship clings to him. But the case of the present petitioner is quite different from the case of Muktar Ahmed inasmuch as he did not continue to be a permanent resident of Bangladesh. 

 26. The next case referred to by the learned Advocate for the petitioner is the case of Abdul Hoque Vs. Govt. of Bangladesh reported in 33 DLR 113 and the same case decided by the Appellate Division and reported as the People's Republic of Bangladesh Vs. Abdul Hoque reported in 1982 BLD (AD) 143. In that case Abdul Hoque was admittedly born in Satkhira within Bangladesh in 1932. He was a permanent resident of Bangladesh on the 25th March, 1971; he resided in the then East Pakistan althrough upto November, 1971 when he had to go to the then West Pakistan and he came back to Bangladesh after the political change in August, 1975. He came to Bangladesh with a Pakistani passport and on his arrival he surrendered the passport and applied for citizenship of Bangladesh; but the Government refused to grant the same and he was asked to leave the country. So he moved this Court by a Writ Petition and their Lordships of the High Court Division on consideration of the facts and circumstances of that case held him to be a Stateless subject who had no nationality. It was held that he cannot be asked to leave the country. On appeal by the Government, their Lordships of the Appellate Division held that High Court Division was not correct in holding that Abdul Hoque was a Stateless person. Their Lordships noticed the factual position of the case. It was not disputed by the Government that Abdul Hoque was born in this country; that he was a permanent resident of Bangladesh on the 25th March, 1971, that he went to the then West Pakistan on a business tour; that he was an indoor patient in a hospital of Karachi for about 8 months and when he came out from hospital the repatriation process ceased. Thus he returned to Bangladesh with a Pakistani passport and surrendered the passport to the Bangladesh Authority; and he applied for citizenship certificate from the Bangladesh Government. The Government having denied the citizenship certificate he filed the writ petition. Their Lordships considered the proviso to Article 2 of PO 149 of 1972 in particular the provision considering the facts of that case held that his temporary absence was covered by the proviso to Article 2 and in the eye of law he remained a resident of Bangladesh. As has been pointed out earlier, the proviso applies to only those categories of persons who in course of his employment or whose dependent for pursuit of his studies was residing in Pakistan and who was prevented from returning to Bangladesh. As a matter of fact Abdul Hoque was a Pan (betel leaf) dealer who used to supply Pan to different dealers in the then West Pakistan and he went to Karachi for collection of his dues. As such their Lordships of the Appellate Division held that his case was covered by the proviso to Article 2. 

 28. The next case referred to by the learned Advocate for the petitioner is the case of Mirza Shahab ispahani Vs. The Government of Bangladesh reported in 40 DLR 87 to the judgment of which one of us was party and the same case decided by the Appellate Division upholding the decision of the High Court Division reported in 40 DLR (AD) 116. The question of citizenship arose in that case incidentally because the property of Mirza Shahab Ispahani was declared as abandoned property. The fact of that case is that Mirza Shahab Ispahani is the son of late Mr. Justice MA Ispahani who retired as the Chief Justice of Dhaka High Court and died in Bangladesh in 1982. He was buried in Dhaka. His son was born in 1941 in Calcutta and while Mr. Justice Ispahani was a District Judge he opted for the then East Pakistan in 1947 and since then Mr. justice Ispahani lived in the then East Pakistan and died there. Mirza Shahab Ispahani while a student was sent to London for prosecuting his studies. He went to England on a passport issued to him from Dhaka which was his permanent address. After his studies he became a Chartered Accountant and had his own earnings in England. He got an allotment of a plot of land at the Gulshan Model Town and built a house thereon. He let out the house to the then Deputy High Commissioner for Britain in Dhaka on a monthly rent. His mother was living in Dhaka and he had a flat at the Ispahani Colony in Dhaka. Finding him absent his property was declared as abandoned 'property. Mirza Shahab Ispahani was holding a Pakistan passport till he surrendered the same on 28.2.72 when he applied for a British passport and he got a British passport on 14.4.1972 valid upto the 13th of May, 1992. The contention of the Government was that he was citizen of Pakistan after the 25th of March, 1971 and as such he was not a citizen of Bangladesh and his property was rightly declared as abandoned property. The High Court Division as well as their Lordships of the Appellate Division held that his case was covered by Article 2A of PO 149 of 1972 which provides that a person to whom Article 2 would have ordinarily applied but for his residence in the United Kingdom shall be deemed to continue to be permanent resident in Bangladesh within the meaning of Article 2. In at case there was no dispute regarding the other qualifications except that he did not continue to be permanent resident of Bangladesh as he had been living in UK since 1952; but Article 2A provides that such resident in United Kingdom shall be deemed to be permanent resident of Bangladesh; in other words, although in actual fact he was residing in UK and was not residing in Bangladesh but by fiction of law he shall be deemed to be permanent resident in Bangladesh. In that case their Lordships further considered the submission of the learned Additional Attorney-General on behalf of the Government that since MS Ispahani was not permanent resident of the territories now comprised in Bangladesh on the 25th March, 1971 he cannot be deemed to be a citizen 'of Bangladesh. This contention, according to their Lordships, was misconceived inasmuch as Article 3 pointedly says that in case of doubt as to whether the person is qualified to be a citizen of Bangladesh under Article 2 the question shall be decided by the Government whose decision shall be final. Their Lordships further noticed that the Government at no stage was called upon to express its view under Article 3. It was further held that the nationality of Mirza Shahab Ispahani was not at issue. In 40 DLR (AD) at page 130 Shahabuddin Ahmed, J (as his Lordship then was) observed as follows: 

 31. In this connection the learned Advocate for the petitioner has referred to the case of Advocate General, Government of East Pakistan, Dhaka Vs. Benoy Bhusan Majumder and others reported in 25 DLR (SC) 9. In that case the respondents after obtaining migration certificate went to India from the then East Pakistan on the 9th December, 1964 from their village home in the District of Bakergonj and they were found in their village in 1967. A case was started against them under section 14 of the Foreigners Act 1946. Their defence was that due to communal disturbances in the then East Pakistan in the year 1964 they temporarily took shelter in India but came back to Pakistan to their village home within a short time when the condition became normal. The trial Magistrate found them guilty of offence under section 14 of the Foreigners Act and on appeal the Sessions Judge, Bakergonj upheld the conviction. On revision to the High Court a learned Single Judge found on evidence that there were communal disturbances in the then East Pakistan in the year 1964 for which the respondents went to Calcutta on the strength of migration certificates, not with the intention of settling there permanently but to take shelter for a temporary period to protect their lives and within a month or two after their entry in India they returned to their house under a border slip. The learned Single Judge held that the respondents who were then admittedly Pakistani citizen before their entry in India did not lose their citizenship by merely crossing into India and staying there for a month or two on the strength of migration certificate. On appeal by the Advocate General of the then Government of East Pakistan, the Supreme Court of Pakistan held that the respondents who were admittedly the citizens of Pakistan before their departure to India did not lose their Pakistani Citizenship by their entry in. India and their temporary stay in that country in the then abnormal situation obtaining in some areas of the then East Pakistan and held that the respondents were not foreigners within the meaning of section 2 (a) of the Foreigners Act. So this case is of no help for the petitioner to hold that temporary physical absence does not discontinue his continuing residence in Bangladesh. 

 "A legislature can certainly give retrospective effect to pieces of legislation passed by it but an executive Government exercising subordinate and delegated powers cannot make legislation retrospective in effect unless that power is expressly conferred. The rule-making authority does not possess plenary power to give the subordinate delegated legislation retrospective operation unless and until that power is expressly conferred by the parent enactment. Hence the rule is well established that even in a case where the executive Government acts as a delegate of legislative authority, it has no plenary power to provide for retrospective operation unless and until that power is expressly conferred by the parent enactment" 

 Relying on this passage the learned Advocate for the petitioner has contended that although Article 3 of the PO 149 of 1972 has been expressly made retrospective in operation from 26.3.1971 but the order contained in the impugned notification dated 18.4.73 cannot act retrospectively. In support of his contention Mr. AR Yusuf, the learned Advocate has referred to five cases of the Indian jurisdiction. The first of which is the case of Modi Food Products Ltd. Vs. The Commissioner of Sales Tax reported in AIR 1956 (All.) 35 wherein a Division Bench of the Allahabad High Court held that a legislature can certainly give retrospective effect to a piece of legislation passed by it but an executive Government exercising subordinate and delegated legislative powers cannot make legislation retrospective in effect unless that power is expressly conferred by the statute. In that case the petitioner was a dealer in non-edible oils. The UP Sales Tax Act came into force with effect from 1.4.48. The petitioner submitted its return for the period from 6.1.1946 to 3.5.1947. There was an amendment of the UP Sales Tax Act by Act No. XXV of 1948 inserting Section 3A by which a higher rate of Sales Tax was authorised and in exercise of the power under the new section 3A the State Government issued notification on 8.6.48 declaring that with effect from 9.4.48 sales tax shall be at the higher rate. It was in that circumstances held that new amendment will not operate retrospectively. Needless to mention that as a general rule taxing statute does not operate retrospectively. The second case in this connection referred to by the learned Advocate for the petitioner is the case of ML Bagga-Vs.  76. The next question that has been raised is the principle of audi alteram partem i.e. the principle of natural justice that no one should be condemned unheard. On this point Mr. AR Yusuf has referred to the cases of the Government of East Pakistan Vs. Nur Mohammad reported in PLD 1964 (SC) 451, Abdur Rahman, Advocate Vs. The Collector and Deputy Commissioner, Bahawalnagar, PLD 1964 (SC) 461, Bangladesh Steamer Agencies Association Vs. Bangladesh, reported in 31 DLR (AD) 271 and Sayiid Abul Ala Moududi Vs. the Government of Pakistan reported in 17 DLR (SC) 209. In the first three cases mentioned above the law that has been laid down is that the principle of natural justice that no one should be condemned unheard should be read in every legislation in the absence of any provision to the contrary contained in the law itself. However, in the case of Sayed Abul Aliz Moududi, 17 DLR (SC) 209 his Lordship Mr. Justice Fazle-Akbar of the Supreme C of Pakistan held: 

 "This rule expressed in the maxim audi alteram partem was fully considered by this Court in Messrs. Farid Sons Ltd., Karachi and another Vs. Government of Pakistan and another and therefore, needs no elaboration. 

 No doubt as far as possible it must be respected in period of calm and even in times of trouble. But certainly it cannot be said that it is merely a technical conception with a fixed content unrelated to time place and circumstances. It is really a matter of procedure and its application must depend on the particular facts and circumstances of the case. What is unfair in one situation may be fair in another. Furthermore, there may be conceivable circumstances in time of emergency in which it might be necessary for the authorities to take immediate action, for example, the activities of an association may be subversive to government and a serious menace to the country. In such circumstances it will be unrealistic to impeach the action of the Government on the ground that the association was not heard. It must be remembered that sometimes because of abnormal conditions, abnormal means are required to cope with them and this justifies the authorities to take immediate action under the law enabling them to do so. Hence taking action in an emergency without observing the maxim audi alteram partem would be a valid exercise of plenary administrative discretion." 

 I am in respectful agreement with the above quoted observations of their Lordships of the Supreme Court of Pakistan and hold that the principle of audi alteram partem is not of universal applicability and the question whether this principle should be applied or not depends upon the nature of the thing to be done, the manner in which it is to be done and the circumstances in which it is to be done. The learned Attorney-General has conceded that the principle of natural justice should be followed as far as practicable whenever any person's right is going to be adversely affected by any action whether by a Court of law or a Tribunal or an Administrative Authority. At the same time, he contended that in the present case this doctrine is not at all applicable in view of the fact that the government by the impugned order did not cancel the citizenship of the petitioner nor deprive him of his citizenship. The government in exercise of the power conferred by Article 3 of PO 149 of 1972 has given a decision only to remove a doubt as to whether the petitioner fulfilled the requirements of Article 2 so as to be treated as a citizen of Bangladesh or not. His second contention is that since the petitioner was not available in the country and his whereabouts were not known to the Government it was impracticable to serve a show cause notice upon him so as to give him an opportunity of being heard. Whatever may be the language of Article 3 of PO 149 of 1972 there is no doubt about the fact that an order passed under this Article declaring a person not qualified to be deemed to be a citizen of Bangladesh in actual effect interferes with his political status which entails some fundamental rights enumerated in the Constitution which are available to a citizen only. Therefore, it is not worthy to say that by the impugned order no right vested in the petitioner was taken away. Next comes the question whether it was practicable to serve a show cause notice upon the petitioner and the other thirty-eight persons to give them chance to defend themselves as against the proposed action. There is no doubt of the fact that the present petitioner at the relevant time was not available in Bangladesh and therefore, it was not physically possible to serve any notice upon him in person. But our laws provide different modes of service, such as service at the last known residence of the person concerned or by publication in official gazette or in some newspapers and these are treated to be valid and legal service of notice. The government could easily publish a show cause notice either in the gazette or in any newspaper or serve the same at the last known residence in Bangladesh of the petitioner. But this has not been done. This is not a case of emergency as it was in the case of Sayed Abul Ala Moududi. A delay of a month or two in taking a decision regarding the political status of the petitioner and the others mentioned in the notification and to cause service of notice in the meantime would not harm anybody or the public interest or the State of Bangladesh. I am, therefore, of opinion that this is not an exceptional case as has been stated by their Lordships Mr. Fazle Akbar and Mr. Hamoodur Rahman JJ and this being an ordinary case without demanding urgent action, a notice should have been issued asking the person concerned to show cause as to why they should not be declared to be not qualified to be citizens of Bangladesh. Failure to do so has rendered the impugned notification repugnant to the principle of natural justice that no one should be condemned unheard. 

 Mr. AR Yusuf has lastly taken the stand that the powers conferred upon the executive government in Article 3 of PO 149 of 1972 is unfettered and unrestricted and therefore, it may be used in a discriminatory way as there is no guide-line laid down either in the Order itself or in the Rules framed thereunder as to how and in what circumstances this power should be exercised. On this point he referred to the case of Dr. Nurul Islam Vs. The Government, 1981 BLD (AD) 140. I do not think it necessary to discuss the facts of that case and the law enunciated (Appellate Division in view of the fact that, in Article 3 of PO 149 of 1972 is not devoid of Iv principle or guide-line. This Article 3 is closely connected and dependent on Article 2 of the said Order and Article 2 lays down the guide-line or the principles or the qualifications which are required for a person in order to be deemed to be qualified as citizen of Bangladesh in case of doubt as to whether a particular the qualifications or is lacking in anyone mentioned in Article 2 then and then only the government can invoke Article 3 and give decision on the point. Therefore, I hold that this Article is not without any principle or guide-line for the exercise of power conferred by it upon the executive government. Therefore, Article 3 is not ultra-vires to Articles 27 and 31 of the Constitution of the People's Republic of Bangladesh. 

 In the instant case no doubt the impugned order disqualifying the petitioner from being deemed to be a citizen of Bangladesh was passed as early as in 1973 and the present writ petition has been filed in March, 1992. So there is a gap of about 19 years. However, the contention of Mr. AR Yusuf is that though the order was issued as early as in 1973 yet no right was threatened till the show cause notice dated 23.3.92 was served upon the petitioner. It is apparent from the writ petition and the other papers that the impugned order, Annexure-B was passed when the petitioner was outside the country. He, after learning about it, had been submitting representation after representation to the executive government for redress of his grievance. Two of his petitions were rejected in 1978 but he was granted visa to visit Bangladesh with a Pakistani passport and immediately after his arrival he surrendered his passport and applied for citizenship on 7.11.78. After lapse of his renewed visa he was not disturbed so far as his stay in Bangladesh was concerned. Rather on 28.1.81 he was asked by the appropriate authority to furnish an affidavit of allegiance which he did the following day. Then there was no reply to his petition. But the Minister-in-charge of the Ministry concerned i.e. the Ministry of Home Affairs, once on 27th May, 1980 and again on 12th January, 1992 made statement in the Parliament to the effect that Prof. Golam Azam's petition for restoration of citizenship was under active consideration of the government. In the meantime, the petitioner was enrolled as voter in the electoral rolls finally published once in 1983 and again in 1990. No doubt the inclusion of the name of the petitioner in the voter list cannot be deemed to have rescinded the Government's Order contained in the impugned notification, Annexure-B dated 18.4.73. But all these facts and circumstances including the inclusion of his name as a voter, Minister's statements in Parliament and top political leaders meeting the petitioner and discussing matters of national importance with him, were sufficient to make the petitioner believe that his petition for restoration of his citizenship was not only under active consideration but under favourable consideration of the Government. Therefore his right to stay in Bangladesh and to exercise the right of franchise an exclusive right of citizens only was not threatened till the notice dated 23.3.92 asking him to show cause why he should not be deported from Bangladesh being a foreigner. Immediately on receipt of this notice the petitioner gave his reply and he being taken into detention moved this Court in its extraordinary original jurisdiction under Article 102 of the Constitution. It should be kept in mind that the Supreme Court has always deprecated the tendency to rush to Court before exhausting available administrative remedies. Under the facts and circumstances of this case I am of the opinion that the present writ petition does not suffer from inordinate delay and that the delay that has occurred has been satisfactorily explained.

 This matter arises out of a notification (Annexure 'B') issued by the Government in exercise of the power under Article 3 of the Bangladesh Citizenship (Temporary Provision) Order, 1972 hereinafter referred to as Citizenship Order, 1972. The notification recites that the decision has been taken under Article 3 of the Order on the ground that these persons have stayed abroad since before liberation of Bangladesh and by their conduct cannot be deemed to be a resident of Bangladesh and that they continued to be a citizen of Pakistan. Those persons were declared disqualified to be the citizens of Bangladesh and those persons included Mr. Hamidul Huq Chowdhury, Mr. AS Saadi, Advocate, Prof. Golam Azam, Mr: Korban Ali, Bar-at-Law, Mr. Nurul Amin, Mr. Mohammad Ali, Mr. Humayun Khan Panni and a numbers of others, in total 38 persons. 

 100. This provision qualifying a person to be deemed to be a citizen or not should be understood and explained within this qualifying clause as in Article 2. Art 3 is not a qualifying clause, rather an enabling clause authorizing the Government of Bangladesh to decide and to decide finally in case of doubt as to whether a person is qualified to be deemed to be a citizen of Bangladesh as under Article 2 of this Order or not. 

 106. The expression "continue to be so resident" as appears in Article 2 obviously means by the application of ejusdem generis rules to mean "so permanently resident" thereafter in Bangladesh as distinguished from the proviso to Article 2 which proviso is added to explain the legislative intention to meet the situation prevailing at that historical moment of this nation's birth along with its ten (10) crores of people, clearly providing for the absentee Bangladeshis resident in Pakistan. This is also in conformity with the generally accepted view of the courts that residence anywhere must be a voluntary residence and not residence out of compulsion which compulsory residence shall bear no consequences. For example, a British soldier who resided out of compulsion in a Nazi Prison Camp in Germany cannot be called an enemy in England for residing on an enemy territory for his property to vest in the Government as enemy property. Now back to the proviso it is seen that the proviso provided that a person who is permanent resident of the territory now Bangladesh but resident in the territory at war with or in military operation against Bangladesh, in connection with studies or service and is prevented from returning to Bangladesh "shall be deemed to be resident in Bangladesh" as in condition number 3 in Article 2(i). The definition relating to student or service holders as in proviso do not appear to be exhaustive but inclusive of hundreds of other Bangladeshis stranded in Pakistan and in fact those hundreds of others were subsequently repatriated officially to Bangladesh long after 16th of December, 1971 as is evident by the tripartite agreement in 1974 among Bangladesh, Pakistan and India which also repatriated 194 war prisoners. 

 108. In the case of Bishal Deo Tewari Vs. The State, reported in 27 DLR 622 a very similar matter came for decision. In that case the petitioner Bishal Deo Tewari was the pujari of Dhakeshwari Mandie at Dhaka. His parent was the sebayet of that Dhakeshwari Deity. It is claimed that the petitioner besides being the owner of a house at 7, Orphanage Road has got other landed properties in Dhaka and a sweetmeat shop and Municipal licence for business at Dhaka. He was arrested under the Foreigners Act as Indian National and detained for an unauthorised entry into Bangladesh' from India. The impugned order issued under the Foreigners Order 1951 by the Civil Authority on 1.7.75 and thereafter detained in Dhaka Central Jail. It has been argued in that case on behalf of Bishal Deo Tewari that he is a national of this country, and also of the then East Pakistan and as such cannot be served with the order under the Foreigners Order, 1951. The Government opposed the Rule by the Government that the petitioner is an Indian National and this impression of the Government was founded upon some correspondence between the Government of Bangladesh and the Indian High Commissioner in Bangladesh. The Division Bench of the Dhaka High Court who heard the matter consisting of Mr. Justice KM Sobhan and Mr. Justice SM Hussain quoted Article 2 of the Presidential Order 149 of 1972 namely the Citizenship Order of 1972, which was the relevant provision in that case and after quoting the provision the Court observed thus: 

 110. Article 2(i), 2(ii) and the proviso thus, covers all, whether physically present or not, but Bangladeshi by birth or permanently domiciled and also persons of Bangladeshi origin who are in temporary residence in Pakistan for service or studies and otherwise and prevented from returning to Bangladesh. Temporary residence in Pakistan would thus, come under the proviso to Article 2 and in the tripartite agreement between Bangladesh, Pakistan and India it was further extended to all "stranded" Bangladeshis in Pakistan, as a Government policy. 

 111. A similar point came for consideration before a Division Bench of this court in the case of Abdul Hoque Vs. Government of Bangladesh, reported in 33 DLR 113 which was subsequently taken to Appellate Division, reported in 1982 BLD (AD) 143. In that case under report, Abdul Hoque admittedly was born in Satkhira within the territory of Bangladesh in 1932. He was a permanent resident admittedly on the territory now comprised in Bangladesh on 25th day of March, 1971. He went to Karachi in November, 1971 which is also the date when Golam Azam left for Lahore to attend a Conference in November, 1971, which is much after the commencing day of Citizenship Ordinance of 1971 on 26th day of March, 1971. Abdul Hoque went to Karachi in November, 1971 to collect dues from Karachi trader dealing in pan business and became ill and was in hospital for 8 months. When he came out of hospital the repatriation of Bangladeshis was over and thus could not come back. He eventually came back to Bangladesh in 1975 with a Pakistani passport as a travel document. He surrendered his Pakistani passport to the Government of Bangladesh and applied for citizenship of Bangladesh which was refused and he was asked to leave the country immediately under the Foreigners Act, 1946. Abdul Hoque challenged this order. The High Court Division observed that he was a stateless person and thus cannot be deported. 

 112. The Government made an appeal before the Appellate Division and their Lordships of the Appellate Division dismissed the appeal filed by the State. It is to be noted that the stand of the Government in that case was that the Government had refused to grant the citizenship of the petitioner as he left this country in November, 1971 as a Collaborator and he came back after 5 years and asked for citizenship which was refused and Government asked him to leave the country. The Appellate Division after quoting Art. 2 of the Citizenship Order of 1972 including the proviso to Art. 2 found that the respondent was born in the territory now comprised in Bangladesh but his temporary absence is covered by the proviso and the proviso provided that he shall be deemed to continue to be resident in Bangladesh notwithstanding his temporary residence in a country which was at war or engaged in military operations against Bangladesh if he was prevented from returning to Bangladesh. The court considered that A. Hoque asserted that he was "prevented" from returning to Bangladesh but the circumstances as mentioned by him in the petition namely that he was in hospital for some time and he was prevented from returning to Bangladesh had not been challenged, The' finding of the Appellate Division is that Abdul Hoque remained a resident of Bangladesh and therefore, the court held that the order of deportation must be declared as not lawfully made and the Government appeal was dismissed. 

 114. A point of similar nature again came up for decision in the case of Mira Shahab Ispahani Vs. Government of Bangladesh, reported in 40 DLR 87. The said case was decided by the Appellate Division upholding the decision of the High Court Division, reported in 40 DLR (AD) 

 116. On an examination of the above 3 decided cases on this qualification clause as under Article Z of the Order including the proviso to Art. 2 it thus, appears that the expression permanent resident as occurred in Article 2 has been distinguished from the expression ordinary resident giving permanent resident the status of domicile as it is understood in International Law when it concerns sovereign State. Their Lordships had also, while examining the proviso to Art. 2 which speaks of a prevention clause, in Abdul Hoque's case extended' the sway of the proviso to all that were resident in Pakistan irrespective of being a student or employed as service holder and is being prevented from returning to Bangladesh and this extension of entry to all Bangalees that were "stranded" in Pakistan is found in the Tripartite Agreement signed on 9th of April, 1971 by the Foreign Ministers of India., Pakistan and Bangladesh which agreement was shown to me by the Attorney-General. It acknowledges the fact that for harmony and reconciliation all the "three governments agreed to complete repatriation of Bangalees from Pakistan, Pakistanis in Bangladesh and the Pakistani prisoners of war in India" and it declared that such civilian repatriation had started in September, 1973 and 3,00,000 had been repatriated and it hoped that the repatriation of prisoners of war would be completed by the end of April, 1974 and because of the progress of this, three-way repatriation started under the Delhi Agreement on 29th August, 1973. Governments of these three countries were gratified that such a large number of persons (in their language) "detained and stranded" in these three countries reached their destination which expression 'stranded" is much wider in term and goes beyond persons prevented. 

 117. From a reading of this Tripartite Agreement signed by Dr. Kamal Hossain for Bangladesh, Swaran Singh for India and Mr. Aziz Ahmed for Pakistan as respective Foreign Ministers it is seen that there it has been stated that as Prime Minister Bhutto had asked the people of Bangladesh to forgive and forget the past crimes and as the Prime Minister of Bangladesh said that he also wanted the people to forget the past and to make a fresh start stating that the people of Bangladesh know how to forgive and having regard to the appeal of the Prime Minister of Pakistan to the people of Bangladesh to forgive and forget the mistakes of the past and the foreign minister of Bangladesh having Slated that the Government of Bangladesh had decided not to proceed with the trial as an act of clemency it was agreed that 195 prisoners of war may be repatriated to Pakistan along with the other prisoners of war now in the process of repatriation under the Delhi Agreement. 

 120.  In the instant case the petitioner was been here and thus, comes under Article 2(i). He stayed in Bangladesh as permanent resident on 25th of March, 1971 and was present here physically on 25th of March and 26th March, 1971 and he continued to be so permanently resident after the commencing day of the Order and the petitioner is not proved to have gone to Pakistan any time after November, 1972 when he left to reside there permanently. He stayed in Pakistan for 11 months and he stated that his stay in Pakistan was against his will. He went to Lahore" on 22.11.71 temporarily to attend his party meeting while his wife, seven children, father and mother all were living at Dhaka (para-14). After 10 days war broke out on 3.12.71 and he started for Dhaka on the same day by aeroplane but the aeroplane carrying him, after reaching near Dhaka could not land at Dhaka Airport because of war. He was taken back to land at Colombo. Thereafter as there was bombing at Karachi Airport, his plane took him along with others to Jeddah, where after they were taken to Karachi. He had to remain in Karachi against his will for 11 months as the then Government of Pakistan did not allow any Bangladeshi to leave Pakistan and while he was unwillingly staying in Pakistan he in the month of March, 1972 tried to go to London but could not get any passport for that but only for Hajj. He obtained a Pakistani passport as travel document and this was done before repatriation had started for Bangladeshi nationals in September, 1973 and when in Mecca he heard that political mispropaganda is high in Bangladesh against him and he was informed that is his life will be at stake if he went back to Bangladesh. (paras 16, 17, 18). There was no Bangladeshi Embassy in Saudi Arabia also then so he went to London in 1st week of April, 1973 when some days thereafter he was disqualified (Para-19). 

 "The contention of the respondent that Mr. Hamidul Huq Choudhury was a citizen of Pakistan was based upon firstly, that he was away from Bangladesh and that by notification dated 18A.1973 the Government declared that Mr. Hamidul Huq Choudhury did not qualify to be a citizen of Bangladesh, Mr. Chowdhury claimed that he never became a citizen of any other state and his citizenship by statutory provision continued to be Bangladeshi. It appears to us on a perusal of notification dated 18.4.73 that prior to the said notification Mr. Hamidul Huq Choudhury by statutory provision was a citizen of Bangladesh. 

 This notification was subsequently declared void by another notification of the Government dated 19.7.77. In this view we hold that Mr. Hamidul Huq Choudhury continued to be a citizen of Bangladesh though he was away from the country" 

 The contention of the Attorney-General that Article 2B(I)(ii) would act as a validation of the impugned notification to correct its error has no basis, as there cannot be any validation by implication but by law itself and more so of a past and closed transaction (Corpus Juris Vol. 59. Pages 1181-1184 & 434-439). Moreover, this added Article 2B(I)(i) would not also be available to the Government to remove a doubt whether a person is qualified to be a citizen of Bangladesh under Art. 2 of the Order, as on the day the notification was issued and made effective on 18.4.73 the amendment made on 19.5.73 was not even born or added to Art. 2. 

 Except this disqualification clause as in Art. 2B (I) added subsequently to the 'Citizenship Order of 1972 as it originally stood, the said Order does not anywhere make any other "conduct" such as treason, sedition, waging war against Government established by law, which are in Penal Code, a disqualification for citizenship. This appears to be a clear and deliberate omission made by the legislature in Citizenship Order 1972 (PO 149 of 1972) at that time the law of Citizenship Order, 1972 was first promulgated on 15th December, 1972 with a retrospective effect from 26th March, 1971. 

 126. This part of the political conduct of the petitioner appears to have been argued at length as the Government affidavit-in-opposition shows before the Division Bench, but Sarker, J on this, at the relevant part of his judgment at pages 24-25, observed as follows: 

 128. I, on my part, would put an end to this by holding as I did before that if Golam Azam is charged for abetting murder, rape or arson in collaboration with Pakistan army or charged for sedition or for treason or for waging war against the Bangladesh Government, he will answer those, but for this citizenship matter those would be irrelevant and being irrelevant I would make no comment further on those allegations, keeping in mind that this Citizenship case centered round Article 2 only and no further. Justice is to be done in accordance with law and any attempt to be wiser than the law is by good law forbidden. 

 130. The petitioner's case had again been that he used a Pakistani passport only as a travel document He never went back to Pakistan thereafter at any point of time to reside there showing allegiance to Pakistan as many others did and if there was. any doubt as to that he ought to have been given a chance to explain his position and thus, there would exist at least a "legitimate expectation" that the government would hear him before they took away that vested right ex parte and, according to Mr. AR Yusuf, even God did not punish or condemn Adam without giving him a hearing. 

 133. The law in this regard is otherwise. For the purpose of natural justice the question which would matter is not whether the applicant has some right but whether any power has been exercised over him to his disadvantage ex parte. It is not a question of right but a matter of exercise of government power in a manner which is just fair, reasonable and considerate. 

 140. I respectfully agree with the above and it needs be mentioned that in Maudoodi's case Government action against Jamaat-e-Islami was taken under the Criminal Law Amendment Act which was enacted for the purpose of prohibiting formation of association dangerous to public peace and section 16 of that Act empowered the Provincial Government to declare any association unlawful if in the opinion of the said government the association constitutes a danger to public peace or had the object of interfering with the maintenance of law and order. 

 In the instant case of Golam Azam the Government while exercising the power under Article 3 of the Citizenship Order of 1972 had not been exercising a "police power" in-an emergency to prevent an immediate unlawful dangerous act threatening public safety or law and order in the country or in a part of the country. But in fact the Government did exercise a power in peace time and exercised the power in disqualifying the petitioner along with 38 others in which Hamidul. Huq Chowdhury topped the list when there was no proved emergency. Government was not acting in an emergency but long after the liberation of Bangladesh and in peace time and in fact no such immediate danger or emergency had even been pleaded in this case by the government nor they made out a case of emergency nor we find any proved emergency. Before this court it was the case of the government that he could not be heard as his" whereabouts were not known" and by giving notice in his collaboration case it had been complied with. Mr. AR Yusuf argued that this is not the correct position as his whereabouts were known to Government and they sent notice at his Maghbazar address in the collaboration case that time to appear and reply. 

 142. It is seen that the Citizenship Order, 1972 had also made no provision for any appeal or for any representation or for any review before any committee and made the decision of the Government [mal. This is finally deciding the matter ex parte, in which case the necessity of hearing him before the final order was passed, closing the door for ever was more urgent. He ought to have been heard in his defence. 

 143. It is true that Article 3 of the Citizenship Order 1972 in case of doubt makes the decision of the government final. It is argued that as the decision in this matter would be regarded to be final this court would not reopen the said finality arrived at by the Government' in issuing the notification. 

 145. There remains the question of delay in filing of this application as pleaded by the respondent Government. Under the law for an aggrieved person to come before this court under Article 102 of the Constitution, no statutory limitation is provided for as in a suit. The jurisdiction under Article 102 of the Constitution is a jurisdiction in law and also in equity. A court thus, entertains a petition if the delay is explained to the satisfaction of the court and it would be explained and examined in the light of the attending facts and circumstances of each case. 

 148. In the instant case the question is whether the petitioner had explained the delay and moved the court in time when his position was actually threatened in the light of decisions as above. It had been stated by the learned Counsel that when Golam Azam left this country in November, 1971 there was no requirement of a passport to travel between East and West. He went to Lahore in November, 1971 when few days thereafter war broke out between India and Pakistan. Pakistan Army thereafter surrendered. Pakistan did not recognize Bangladesh for some time and the petitioner could not get a travel document from Pakistan to come out of that country or to travel to Bangladesh and then repatriation had not started. So out of necessity he had to obtain a Pakistani passport and with that document he went to Saudi Arabia in November, 1972 only for Hajj and thereafter he went to London in April, 1973 when few days thereafter he was disqualified from being a citizen of Bangladesh. He was not able to come back to Bangladesh because of this political rivalry with the party in power. He had fear of his life and therefore was prevented from coming to Bangladesh. During those days, according to him, he would not get any redress even if he would apply. Thereafter there was change of government in 1975 and in the year 1976 he was again faced with a Notification dated 17.l.76 (Annexure-D) issued by the then Government of Bangladesh asking those persons whose citizenship have been previously" cancelled" to apply for it. He applied for it. There was no reply. A reminder (Annexure-D 1) dated 12.l.77 was sent by him from London and he got a reply (Annexure-E) dated 23.4.77 in which his application was not accepted which he received in London. During those days there was Martial Law in the country and also a state of Emergency proclaimed much earlier on 28th of December, 1974 and because of which emergency fundamental rights as in Arts. 27, 31, 32, 33, 35, 36, 37, 38, 39,40 and 42 were suspended by that emergency, proclaimed by President Mohammadullah and this proclamation of emergency continued throughout the successive governments till it was withdrawn by another proclamation on 27th November, 1979. 

 150. I have given my anxious consideration to the submissions made by the petitioner's lawyer before this court and find that the petitioner's application did not suffer from any sheer negligence to assert a right no' he was indolent or callous. He was hoping to get it and his right was re-offered by Government again in 1974 after he was disqualified in 1973 when things in Bangladesh was against him and fundamental rights suspended. He applied twice, his matter was in the process of being considered on either way as stated in Parliament Leaders in power met him for his party's support, his name appeared in voters list. He was here for long hoping to get registration when he was served with the deportation notice and immediately he came to the Court. In the process no right had accrued to a third party and if his application is heard no prejudice would be caused to the right of any innocent third party. I agree with BJ Chowdhury J when he held that this petition is not so delayed as to be not maintainable. 

 151. On the premises above I thus, find the writ to be maintainable and having found on merits that the petitioner is a citizen of Bangladesh by birth within Article 2 of the Order and also prevented from returning to Bangladesh for some time as under the Proviso to Article 2 of the Citizenship Order, he cannot be treated as a foreigner, he being a citizen of Bangladesh and cannot, therefore, be ordered to show cause as to why he should not be deported from Bangladesh (Annexure-K) and this notice having been issued without lawful authority to a citizen of Bangladesh, is therefore, declared to be illegal and without lawful authority. Consequently, the disqualification notification as issued by the previous Government on 18.4.73 (Annexure-B) is also declared to be bad in law because initially it was ordered in violation of the principle of natural justice against a person who by statutory provision was then a citizen and acting in excess of jurisdiction by travelling beyond Article 2 as it stood on the notification day, thereby rendering the proceeding in passing the notification dated 18.4.73 coram non judice rendering the whole order void ab initio being without jurisdiction.
